title: A new meta-analysis says the effect is much bigger. Here is how I decided not to use it.
finalText:
A new study landed that would make my argument easier to sell.

I am not going to use it that way.

The paper is a peer reviewed meta analysis of social media use and adolescent mental health. It reports a pooled correlation of r = 0.308.

If you already believe social media is harming children that might sound like the confirmation you have been waiting for, and I build something for parents who are worried about exactly this, so a number like that would suit me.

Which is why I read past it.

The analysis pools 12 studies contributing 15 effect sizes, and it reports heterogeneity of I squared = 93.85 percent. Put plainly, the studies inside it disagree with each other so much that averaging them tells you very little about any one of them, and nothing about your own child.

Two more things.

A correlation is not proof that social media caused anything. And one pooled measure of social media use cannot tell us what a particular child watched, who they spoke to, what happened at bedtime, or what else was going on in their life.

The authors also report differences across school stages. That is worth investigating. It is not a sound basis for calling younger children the most vulnerable.

The summary does not say which countries the studies come from, so I would not carry any of it across to children here.

None of that makes the paper wrong. It deserves to be read and set beside the other evidence. But a result that points the way I would like deserves the same scrutiny as one that does not. Probably more.

It is the reason the stage check we built asks three questions about one child, yours, and promises nothing about what happens next.

The paper is linked in the comments.

If this is how you want evidence handled, repost it. The response should be in proportion to the evidence, and that has to cut both ways.

When did you last turn down a number that suited you?
firstComment:
The paper: https://doi.org/10.1177/13591045261487468

The strongest objection is that a peer reviewed meta analysis is still useful evidence even when its studies differ. Agreed. I am not rejecting the paper or the correlation it reports. My caution is about treating a pool of correlational studies that disagree this much as a settled answer about any one child.
